title: Theory and Practice of Muslim State in India
byline: by K.S. Lal · Aditya Prakashan, New Delhi · 1999
lede: Fifty years after his first article on the subject (October 1947), Lal sets out what he says earlier histories, his own included, left out. Instead of describing the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) and the Mughal empire (1526–1707) from the chronicles alone, he sets their administration against Islamic scripture and law: the Quran, the Hadis, the biographies of the Prophet and the Shariat. His claim is that kings and conquerors acted largely as those texts directed. He follows the state through its duties, its income and its spending, then argues the same ideas shape Muslim politics in India today, and closes with a long reply to his reviewers.
facts: duties of the Islamic ruler, per Ruben Levy: justice, taxation, Friday prayer, jihad

khums: the state's share of war booty
Lal's half-century of writing on the Muslim state
note: Lal argues that Islamic doctrine shaped how Muslim rulers in India governed. Other historians weigh politics, economics and local custom more heavily. His interpretation is summarised here as his.
